O Death, may the twenty-two, four, five, one, and nine syllables, as well as the ten, the visargas, the five, the one, and the sixteen,
along with the one in the sixth, be auspicious for you.
The *aśmanvatī* [verse] consists of twenty-one; the *vṛtra* [section] consists of four;
the fourteenth is the beginning of the *apādya*; the two *vṛddhi*s are said to be in the three [sections]; however, on the ninth day, there is an ox (*anaḍvān*), and in the sixth, there is a *vṛc*.
Eighteen for you, O Agni; three for the three, and three for two—that makes nineteen. One for the living, and one chosen as the fifth;
one for the highest goal on the fourteenth day, and three for unity.
On the seventeenth [verse], [one recites] *kavyādam*; on the fifth, *vṛcca*; on the fourth, *ekatā vaha vapām*; and on the twentieth, the fourth [section].
Then, on the fourteenth, one recites seven [verses] and three in sequence; with the fourteenth verse, *syonā pṛthivī*, [one concludes] for two [sections] by means of four [verses].
"From this [hymn] of thirteen [verses], for the two [deities], there are three discharges of breath.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the *Padakārikāratnamālā* on the *Vājasaneyisaṃhitā*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter:
the *Ṛca*, the *Vāc*, the eighteen, and those three well-known ones;
that which is my deficiency, the nineteen, and the seven well-known ones [accompanied] by two.
By which [verse] do we [attain] the twelfth? One, two, and one;
Indra, the king of all, eight; the occurrence in two by three;
then Mitra and Varuṇa become eight; one occurs in six, well-known.
The *vāta* hymn purifies with nine verses; the fourth [section] likewise has four emissions;
the fifth has eighteen verses and four *vṛc*s;
and the fourth [section] has ten well-known goddesses for the sake of prosperity.
*dyauḥ śāntiḥ* ends with the ninth [syllable], and likewise there are six *visargas*.
In *dhṛte*, *dṛm̐ ha māmitrasya padāstu* consists of twenty-one [syllables].
If *jyok ca sandru syaṣṭamyām* occurs, there would be an increase of two [syllables].
Salutations to you! From whichever [direction] the four, three, and one reach the tenth,
and from whichever [direction] the three reach the fourteenth, and here with the eight on the thirteenth— therein, that eye is in the enclosure of the two, and in the two, it is spread abroad.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the *Padakārikāratnamālā* on the Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya;
now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Nārī took four [of them] right there, while Visruta took one;
on the fourteenth day, Devī Dyāvā took three, and in two [cases], Vṛta took two from the Visrus;
the Devīs Vamryas took one of six, and likewise four.

In this [verse], at the beginning, the fifth [syllable] is desired; and in the *visruta* [meter], one [syllable] is desired for Indra’s vigor (*ojas*). Or, as in the case of two *visruta*s with five [syllables each], so too [should it be]:
let the *brahman* proceed with sixteen [syllables], one *vṛt* [syllable], and four *visruk* [syllables].
With six [verses], one cuts off the head of Makha; with two, the two ears; likewise, on the fourteenth day, with two [verses], one cuts off the horse; with four [verses], the tail;
and with one [verse], "For the upright and virtuous you," one cuts off the fourth part.
The *yamā* and *yamakhāyaṃ* are seventeen; there is one [syllable] in the sixth *vṛt*;
the *anādhṛṣṭā* are forty-four at the beginning.
The *veṣṭanā* are to be known as ten, and the *visargā* are twenty.
"svāhā" with the Maruts is the ninth; likewise, there are two of three syllables each; "devānām piteka" has fourteen syllables; "trayo visruk" has twenty-one syllables;
and "samagnirvisargā" consists of exactly two [syllables].
The upholder of heaven, Viṣṇu, shall destroy the Vṛtras; Śali shall slay them.
Then Aṅga shall see them; the eighteen, the three, and the seven who have gone astray—Viśvāsa shall slay these twenty-nine, and Pañcaika one.
"Thou art our father; twenty-three [days] for two [months]; five [days] for two [months] ending with the night;
with the banner of the day on the twelfth [lunar day]; four [days] with the enclosure; and Visruk"—thus [ends] the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
The thirty-seventh chapter in the *Padakārikāraṇtamālā*.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter:
"And having omitted the end of the *gāṇa* in the fifteenth [chapter] from these two."
The *ila* verse begins with *ehy ādi*; likewise, there are eleven *padās*.
On the ninth day, there is the *ādityai rāsnā*; for the two Aśvins, there is *pinvasva*, as well as the *aveṣṭana* and *astra*.
"That breast of yours" (*yaste stanaḥ*) consists of twenty verses; furthermore, there are five *vṛts* and eleven [verses].

The Gāyatra [meter] consists of twenty-four syllables; in two [verses] there is the Vṛhatī, and three Visruks. When there are nine, it is the Samudra; when one is found, it is the Savitṛ. In six [syllables] there are four, and the Vṛhatī always exists.
In the sacrifice to Yama and Aṅgiras, there is one *vṛta* for each; in the twelve [verses] to the Viśvedevas, two for each; likewise, three for two [deities];
on the thirteenth day, there are two types, and the fourth is a single *vṛca*.
The Aśvins drank the Gharma with ten [verses]; one [verse] was drunk by four who were spread out.
The Aśvins drank ten; Vṛcīka drank one, and Ekavimśati-drinker drank one.
Make swell for nourishment, O daughter of Ṣaṣṭhī; ten [verses] are praised, then two, and then the intermediate one.
*svāhā pūṣṇaḥ* on the eleventh [day], with five verses; *aṣṭa nisrutāḥ*; *rudrā yaḥ rudra hataye* with two sets of seventeen [verses] for the two [days];
and *abhīmam mahaḥ* on the eleventh [day]—one [verse] is chosen for all three [days].
The four-cornered [verse] is on the fifteenth; likewise, the sixfold and the elevenfold [verses] are on the eleventh.

"O Gharma, this is for thee" is on the fifth. Where the end of the group is not stated, it is on the twelfth. "The bull has bellowed" is on the two; the fivefold and the single [verse] are on the sixth.
As many as there are [verses] on the seventeenth day, three on the twenty-first,
twenty-six on the twenty-second, four on the twenty-fifth, and the fifth [day] has four;
the splendors are joined on the fifteenth, nine on the twenty-third, and four are scattered.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the *Padakārikāratnamālā* on the *Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
"SVĀHĀ to the vital breaths!"—at the time of the *pada* recitation, the sixteenth [verse] is seen as the fourth; from three [verses], five flow forth. "To Speech!
To Breath!"—the fifteenth [verse] is for the mind, one [verse] is for desire, and five flow forth.

The twenty-sixth is Prajāpati; the eleven are those being gathered, while the seventeen are known as the Visargas; likewise, there is one without an end, and Savitṛ is the first of the twenty-six, with the Visrūks being eleven and one.
*Ugra* with ten, *bhīma* with eleven,
*vṛtra* with five, *agni* with twenty, [the hymn] with the heart with six,
*visruk* with two, *ugra* with twenty, and *lohita* with seven, five, and one.
To the body hairs, Svāhā! On the eleventh day, four; on the fifth, to Āyāsa, eight; and likewise four to Vṛt.
To Tapas, six; and one to Vṛta, and indeed Ekata.
"Yamāya antakāya" on the eighth [verse], and "vṛka ekaṃ tu dvayoḥ visruk" [is the rule];
thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the *Padakārikāratnamālā* on the *Vājasaneyisaṃhitā*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
Now begins the fortieth chapter:
while performing the seventeenth [verse] of the *Īśāvāsya*, one should likewise perform the two *visrug* offerings according to the rule,
as well as the single *nāntaka* at the end of the seventeenth.
The seventeenth [verse] is named *asuryā*, consisting of three *vṛtti*s, five *eka*nān, one *anejat*, twenty *viśruk*s, five *tri*nāntakas, and one *antaka*.
That moves by means of the fourteenth; there are two *vṛti*s and two *visruta*s.
He who [recites] all fourteen [verses], or two, or two and one;
in which there are fourteen, or three times six, or six and one; ten in the fourth, and seven and one in the seventh.
The fifteenth [day] is blinding darkness; the threefold one has five streams.
The fourteenth is another deity, as is the one with three revolutions.
The fifteenth is both knowledge and ignorance, and ignorance is a single stream.
On the fifteenth day, five branches of the *prapañca* are renowned; on the fourteenth day, they are different, with three branches and three being renowned;
and on the fifteenth day, there is *sabhūti*, with four branches and one being renowned.
On the thirteenth [syllable], there are two in the golden [vowel] and one surrounded by two; Pūṣan has twenty-five, and Yama has three surrounded by one;
four are "flowing forth," and two are "not final" as enjoined by the sacred revelation.
"Vāyu [is] anila, in the sixteenth [verse], [occurring] three times, once, and once.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled *Ratnamālā*, a commentary on the word-division (*padapāṭha*) of the *Vājasaneyisaṃhitā*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
Visarga, visruk, visrutau, as well as visruta, visruka, visruta, visarjana, visargaka,
and visarjanīya— these are the designations for those things that are to be emitted.

The *śuṅga* is like a young calf; the *bālikā* is like a pair of breasts; the *hu* is like an eye; the *tvaṣṭa* is like a serpent; and the *savi* is known as *ma*. *Veṣṭana* and *veṣṭana* are both [designations for] the enclosure, while *vṛd* and *vela* are said to be the growth.

There are those ending in *n*, as well as those ending in *m*; these words ending in *n* should be known as the designations for the *n*-finals. Likewise, there are the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), the circumflex (*svarita*), and the monotone (*pracaya*).

When the phonemes are divided into three parts within a common location such as the throat (kaṇṭha) and so forth, they are produced there; among them, that which arises in the upper portion is to be known as the acute (udātta), while that which is low is the grave (anudātta).
The anudātta (unaccented) is to be recognized as such, while the svarita (circumflex) follows after it;
the wise know that the svarita is a combination of high and low pitches.
Like the udātta, it occurs in saṃhitā (continuous recitation), but in the case of individual words (pada-kāla), they are placed [as unaccented].
All the *sarva-varṇas* are indeed placed [therein], and a *pracaya* is seen;
those syllables which follow a *svarita* are known as *pracaya*.
[Examples are]: *sādanyam*, *sudhukṣam*, *sīṣadhīdhi*, and *saduṣṭaraḥ*.
There is no grasping among these; the Nishada does not [sing] with the Pravaṇas.
There are eight places for the articulation of the phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.

One should know that the letter *ha* when joined with the fifth [consonants] and with the labials (*anasthā*) is dental (*urasya*); when uncombined, they say it is guttural (*kaṇṭhya*). Furthermore, there are four efforts (*prayatna*) for all phonemes in the same manner.
There are the qualities of *spṛṣṭa* (contacted) and *īṣatspṛṣṭa* (slightly contacted), as well as *saṃvṛta* (closed) and *vivṛta* (open).

A short vowel (*hrasva*) consists of one measure (*mātra*), a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is said to consist of two measures, and a protracted vowel (*pluta*) should be known to consist of three measures; a consonant (*vyañjana*), however, consists of half a measure.

The blue jay cries out with one mora, the crow speaks with two moras, and the peacock calls with three moras; such is the definition of a mora. However, when the time for the division of words (pada-kāla) arrives, if it occurs at the end of a metrical foot (gaṇa), it is elided.
Kātyāyana himself [composed] a Sūtra on the Kāyāyana [work], omitting three words or even one word from the many original sources;
after him came Karkī, then Dhanvī, and Vāsudeva was the fifth.
Where *gaṇa*-finals occur, the redundant [syllable] is elided; however,
in the Vājasaneyaka Veda, a redundant syllable becomes a *gaṇa*-final,
for an *anusvāra* preceded by a short vowel becomes a long *anusvāra*.
If there is no subsequent doubling at the time of the sequence of the vowels,
then for *savitḥ*, when there is again a triple *repha* (*r*),
the following should be a *visarjanīya*; in its absence, however, there is an encircling (*veṣṭana*).
This altar is for the sake of vigor, Svāhā! And the two [sides] and the two [spaces], having abandoned them;
there is indeed non-existence in that wrapping, but in that case the wrapping would be otherwise.
Thus, having excluded the inner half and the beyond, it is turned otherwise.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled the *Ratnamālā*, a manual on word-divisions (*padakārikā*) for the *Vājasaneyisaṃhitā*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
